procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 18th May, 2024, dismissing a petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants filed a petition under Section 482, Cr. PC. This petition was dismissed by the High Court on the ground that an earlier petition under the same section had been withdrawn without obtaining leave to file afresh, making the subsequent petition not maintainable.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court considered whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the subsequent petition. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, holding that the High Court was unjustified in dismissing the subsequent petition.

decision.appeal_result: Appeal allowed to the extent as mentioned above.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing a subsequent petition under Section 482 of the Cr.PC on the ground that an earlier petition had been withdrawn without obtaining liberty to file a fresh one.

facts: The appellants were convicted under the Negotiable Instruments Act and, in their appeal, were directed to deposit 20% of the compensation amount.
They challenged this deposit order in the High Court through a petition under Section 482 of the Cr.PC.
This initial petition was dismissed as withdrawn because a prevailing Supreme Court judgment (Surinder Singh Deswal's case) held that such a deposit was mandatory.
Subsequently, the Supreme Court, in another case (Jamboo Bhandari's case), clarified that the deposit might not be mandatory in exceptional cases.
Relying on this change in the interpretation of the law, the appellants filed a second, or subsequent, petition under Section 482.
The High Court dismissed this second petition on the sole ground that the first one had been withdrawn without obtaining permission ('liberty') to file a fresh one.
law: The principle of res judicata (a matter already decided cannot be re-litigated) does not apply to criminal proceedings.
Section 482 of the Cr.PC grants inherent power to the High Court to make orders necessary to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.
There is no blanket rule or absolute bar against filing a successive petition under Section 482.
A subsequent petition under Section 482 is maintainable if there has been a change in facts or circumstances.
A change in the law itself can be considered a 'vital change in circumstance' that justifies entertaining a subsequent petition.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court took a 'constricted view' and was unjustified in dismissing the petition simply because the earlier one was withdrawn without liberty to refile.

The Court reasoned that the appellants filed the second petition not to re-argue the same facts, but because the legal landscape had changed with the new interpretation of the law in Jamboo Bhandari's case.
This change in law was a 'vital change in circumstance' that gave the High Court the power and jurisdiction to hear the new petition.

The appellants were not attempting a 'review in disguise' but were legitimately seeking to have the current law applied to their case to secure the ends of justice, which is the core purpose of Section 482.
Therefore, the subsequent petition was maintainable.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's reasoning, holding that it was unjustified in dismissing the subsequent petition. The Court concluded that a change in the interpretation of the law constitutes a valid new circumstance, making a subsequent petition under Section 482 maintainable, even if a prior petition was withdrawn without obtaining liberty to file a fresh one. The High Court's order was set aside.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing a subsequent petition under Section 482 of the Cr.PC on the ground that an earlier petition had been withdrawn without obtaining liberty to file a fresh one.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was not justified in dismissing the subsequent petition merely because the earlier one was withdrawn without obtaining leave to file a fresh one.

The earlier petition was withdrawn because the High Court was bound by a specific precedent at the time (Surinder Singh Deswal), making the arguments futile in that forum, not because the case lacked merit.
A subsequent petition under Section 482 Cr.PC should be maintainable if it is necessary to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.
respondent_arguments: The subsequent petition was not maintainable because the appellants had withdrawn the earlier petition without obtaining the court's permission (leave) to file a new one on the same issue.

cases.case_name: Surinder Singh Deswal @ Col. S. S. Deswal v. Virender Gandhi
cases.principle: It is the binding precedent on the interpretation of Section 148 of the NI Act over the decision in Jamboo Bhandari, as it was decided by a later bench of co-equal strength that had considered the former.

cases.case_name: Jamboo Bhandari v. Madhya Pradesh State Industrial Development Corporation Ltd. and Ors.
cases.principle: An Appellate Court has limited discretion under Section 148 of the NI Act and may make an exception to the condition of deposit if it is satisfied that the condition would be unjust or would amount to a deprivation of the appellant's right of appeal, for reasons to be specifically recorded.

cases.case_name: S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla
cases.principle: In statutory construction, the substance, rather than the form, is relevant, and it is ultimately a matter of construction of the statute in question that is decisive.

The use of verbs 'may' and 'shall' in a statute is not a sure index for determining whether it is mandatory or directory. The court must gather the real intention of the legislature by carefully analysing the entire statute, as a provision that appears directory in form could be mandatory in substance.

cases.case_name: Reserve Bank of India v. Peerless General Finance & Investment Co. Ltd.
cases.principle: Statutory interpretation must depend on both text and context. The enactment must be viewed as a whole to discover the meaning and placement of each section, clause, and word within the entire scheme of the statute.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When interpreting a statute, the verb 'may' ordinarily implies discretion. Specifically, under Section 148 of the NI Act, while an Appellate Court should normally impose the condition of a deposit, it has the discretion to make an exception. An exception can be made, for reasons to be specifically recorded, if the court is satisfied that the deposit condition would be unjust or would amount to a deprivation of the appellant's right of appeal.
obiter: The principle of res judicata does not apply in a criminal proceeding.
When two benches of co-equal strength render conflicting decisions, the decision of the latter bench is the law.
Statutory interpretation must depend on the text and the context, and the enactment must be looked at as a whole, so that every word has a place and everything is in its place.

The substance, rather than the form, of a statute is relevant, and the use of 'may' or 'shall' is not a sure index of whether a provision is mandatory or directory; the legislative intent must be gathered from the entire enactment.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court was unjustified in dismissing the subsequent petition on the ground that the appellants had withdrawn the earlier petition without obtaining leave to file afresh. The principle of res judicata does not apply to criminal proceedings. A change of law can be considered a vital change in circumstance, which gives the High Court the power and jurisdiction to entertain a subsequent petition to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.
legal_tests_applied: The principle that res judicata has no application in a criminal proceeding.
A subsequent petition under Section 482 Cr.PC is maintainable if the court is satisfied that the order is necessary to prevent abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.
A change of law can be regarded as a vital change in circumstance that justifies entertaining a subsequent petition.
policy_considerations: A subsequent petition under Section 482 Cr.PC should be allowed, despite a previous withdrawal without leave, when it is necessary to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.
